examples.question_text: Express $^{13}C_{4}+{}^{13}C_{5}$ as a single binomial coefficient.
examples.solution_text:
The upper indices match and the lower indices are consecutive. Apply Pascal's identity.
$^{13}C_{4}+{}^{13}C_{5}={}^{14}C_{5}$

examples.question_text: Express $^{28}C_{6}+{}^{28}C_{7}+{}^{29}C_{21}$ as a single binomial coefficient $^{n}C_{r}$ with $r\le n/2$.
examples.solution_text:
Use symmetry to rewrite the third coefficient.
$^{29}C_{21}={}^{29}C_{8}$
Apply Pascal's identity twice.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}{}^{28}C_{6}+{}^{28}C_{7}+{}^{29}C_{21}\\&={}^{29}C_{7}+{}^{29}C_{8}\\&={}^{30}C_{8}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: For integers $n$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le n$, express $^{n}C_{r}+2{}^{n}C_{r-1}+{}^{n}C_{r-2}$ as a single binomial coefficient.
examples.solution_text:
Split the middle term between two adjacent pairs, then apply Pascal's identity twice.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}{}^{n}C_{r}+2{}^{n}C_{r-1}+{}^{n}C_{r-2}\\&=({}^{n}C_{r}+{}^{n}C_{r-1})+({}^{n}C_{r-1}+{}^{n}C_{r-2})\\&={}^{n+1}C_{r}+{}^{n+1}C_{r-1}\\&={}^{n+2}C_{r}\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: For integers $n$ and $r$ with $3\le r\le n$, express $^{n}C_{r}+3{}^{n}C_{r-1}+3{}^{n}C_{r-2}+{}^{n}C_{r-3}$ as a single binomial coefficient.
For integers $n$ and $r$ with $2\le r\le n$, express $^{n}C_{r}+2{}^{n}C_{n-r+1}+{}^{n}C_{n-r+2}$ as a single binomial coefficient.
examples.solution_text:
Use symmetry to obtain consecutive lower indices.
$^{n}C_{n-r+1}={}^{n}C_{r-1}$ and $^{n}C_{n-r+2}={}^{n}C_{r-2}$.
Split the middle term and apply Pascal's identity twice.
$\begin{aligned}&\mathrel{\phantom{=}}{}^{n}C_{r}+2{}^{n}C_{n-r+1}+{}^{n}C_{n-r+2}\\&={}^{n}C_{r}+2{}^{n}C_{r-1}+{}^{n}C_{r-2}\\&=({}^{n}C_{r}+{}^{n}C_{r-1})+({}^{n}C_{r-1}+{}^{n}C_{r-2})\\&={}^{n+1}C_{r}+{}^{n+1}C_{r-1}\\&={}^{n+2}C_{r}\end{aligned}$

examples.derivation: Pascal's identity combines row 13, indices 4 and 5, into row 14, index 5: binom(13,4)+binom(13,5)=binom(14,5). This adapts Development Question 6(e) with different values.

Symmetry gives binom(29,21)=binom(29,8). Pascal gives binom(28,6)+binom(28,7)=binom(29,7), then binom(29,7)+binom(29,8)=binom(30,8). The required bound holds: 8<=15. This follows Exam Question 6's symmetry and repeated-Pascal method.

Splitting the multiplier 2 produces adjacent pairs with lower indices (r,r-1) and (r-1,r-2). They combine to binom(n+1,r)+binom(n+1,r-1)=binom(n+2,r). The stated bounds make every coefficient and application valid, including r=2 and r=n.

The first regrouping preserves multiplicities 1,3,3,1 and combines to binom(n+1,r)+2binom(n+1,r-1)+binom(n+1,r-2). A second regrouping gives binom(n+2,r)+binom(n+2,r-1), then binom(n+3,r). All indices are valid for 3<=r<=n. Only repeated use of the supplied Pascal identity is required.

Symmetry changes lower indices n-r+1 and n-r+2 to r-1 and r-2. Splitting the multiplier 2 then gives binom(n+1,r)+binom(n+1,r-1)=binom(n+2,r). The stated bounds validate the original and transformed indices. This combines the supplied symmetry and repeated-Pascal methods.
